name: Accounting
areas: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Reporting and balance day adjustments
Unit 4 AoS 1 — Extension of recording and reporting
Unit 4 AoS 2 — Analysis and decision making
source: Adapted revision checklist based on VCAA's VCE Accounting Study Design, Units 3 and 4, covering a single activity sole trader trading business. Checklist numbers are internal tracker IDs, not VCAA syllabus numbering.
practiceNote: These practice questions and marking guides are original revision exercises, not VCAA examination questions. Use class resources and past examinations for official practice.
papers: Use the VCAA examination specifications, past examinations and examination reports for official assessment resources.

points.title: The accounting entity and accrual assumptions
points.detail: Recording the records of the business separately from those of the owner, and recognising revenues and expenses when they occur rather than when cash moves.

questions.q: Explain the accounting entity assumption and the accrual basis assumption, giving one example of each.
answer: The accounting entity assumption requires the records of the business to be kept separately from the personal records of the owner.
For example, the owner taking cash for personal use is recorded as drawings rather than as a business expense.
The accrual basis assumption requires revenues to be recognised when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash is received or paid.
For example, a credit sale is recognised as revenue at the date of sale, not at the date the debtor pays.

points.title: Going concern and period assumptions
points.detail: Assuming the business will continue to operate indefinitely, and dividing its life into equal reporting periods so performance can be compared.

questions.q: Explain the going concern assumption and state one consequence for the way assets are reported.
answer: The going concern assumption presumes the business will continue operating into the foreseeable future and will not be wound up.
Non-current assets are therefore reported at their historical cost less accumulated depreciation, reflecting continued use in the business.
They are not reported at the amount that could be obtained in a forced sale, because no such sale is anticipated.

points.title: Qualitative characteristics
points.detail: Relevance, faithful representation, comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability, and the way they guide reporting decisions.

questions.q: Explain relevance and faithful representation, and describe the tension that can arise between timeliness and verifiability.
answer: Relevance requires that financial information be capable of making a difference to the decisions of users, including material information only.
Faithful representation requires that information be complete, neutral and free from material error, corresponding to the real transaction.
Timeliness requires information to be available early enough to influence a decision.
Verifiability requires independent observers to reach consensus, which may require waiting for confirming evidence, so reporting quickly can reduce the confidence in the information.

points.title: Elements of the reports
points.detail: Definitions of assets, liabilities, owner's equity, revenues and expenses, and the classification of each as current or non-current.

questions.q: Define an asset and a liability, and explain the basis on which each is classified as current or non-current.
answer: An asset is a present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events, with the potential to produce economic benefits.
A liability is a present obligation of the entity to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events.
An item is current if it is expected to be converted to cash, sold, consumed or settled within 12 months of the reporting date.
Anything expected to remain beyond 12 months is classified as non-current, which is why a loan's next 12 months of repayments are separated out.

points.title: Source documents
points.detail: Sales and purchase invoices, receipts, cheque butts or EFT records, memos, bank statements and credit notes, and the verification they provide.

questions.q: Name three source documents and state the transaction each verifies.
answer: A sales invoice verifies a credit sale of inventory to a customer.
A receipt verifies cash received, for example from a debtor or a cash sale.
A memo verifies an internal transaction with no external party, such as depreciation, drawings of inventory or an inventory write-down.

points.title: The accounting equation and double entry
points.detail: Assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity, and the requirement that every transaction affect at least two items so the equation remains in balance.

questions.q: State the effect on the accounting equation of purchasing inventory on credit for 4400 dollars including GST.
answer: Inventory increases by 4000 dollars, being the GST-exclusive cost.
The GST clearing account is affected by 400 dollars, reducing the net amount owed to the tax authority or increasing the amount receivable.
Creditors, a liability, increase by the full 4400 dollars.
Total assets increase by 4400 dollars and total liabilities increase by 4400 dollars, so the equation remains in balance.

points.title: The General Journal
points.detail: Recording transactions in journal form with debits before credits, appropriate narrations and correct treatment of GST.

questions.q: Explain the structure of a General Journal entry and why a narration is required.
answer: The debit entry or entries are recorded first, with the credit entry or entries indented beneath them.
The total debits must equal the total credits for every entry.
A narration briefly describes the transaction and identifies the source document that verifies it.
The narration supports verifiability by allowing an independent party to trace the entry back to its supporting evidence.

points.title: The General Ledger
points.detail: Posting from the journal to ledger accounts, the use of cross-references, and balancing accounts at the end of the period.

questions.q: Explain the purpose of the cross-reference in a ledger account.
answer: The cross-reference names the other account affected by the same transaction.
It allows a reader to trace the double entry from one account to its corresponding account.
This supports verifiability and makes errors easier to locate when the ledger does not balance.

points.title: Subsidiary ledgers and schedules
points.detail: Maintaining individual debtor, creditor and inventory records, and reconciling their totals with the control accounts in the General Ledger.

questions.q: Explain the relationship between the Debtors Control account and the debtors subsidiary ledger, and what a difference between them indicates.
answer: The Debtors Control account in the General Ledger records the total amount owed by all credit customers.
The subsidiary ledger contains a separate account for each individual debtor, showing what that customer owes.
The sum of the individual balances in the subsidiary ledger should equal the balance of the control account.
A difference indicates a recording error, such as posting to the wrong debtor or omitting a posting, and must be investigated before reports are prepared.

points.title: The perpetual inventory system
points.detail: Recording inventory movements continuously at cost, the dual entry required for sales, and the role of physical stocktakes.

questions.q: Explain why a credit sale of inventory requires two entries under a perpetual inventory system.
answer: The first entry records the revenue: Debtors Control is debited, and Sales and GST Clearing are credited at the selling price.
The second entry records the expense and the reduction in the asset: Cost of Sales is debited and Inventory is credited at cost price.
Two entries are required because the selling price and the cost price are different amounts recording different effects.
This allows gross profit to be determined and the inventory asset to be stated at cost at all times.

points.title: Inventory cost assignment
points.detail: The first in first out method and the identified cost method, the circumstances in which each is appropriate, and the effect of each on cost of sales.

questions.q: Compare the FIFO and identified cost methods and state when each is appropriate.
answer: FIFO assumes the earliest units purchased are the first sold, so cost of sales is based on the oldest costs and closing inventory reflects the most recent costs.
Identified cost tracks the actual cost of each specific unit sold, usually by serial number or individual tag.
Identified cost suits high-value, individually distinguishable items such as vehicles or machinery.
FIFO suits homogeneous, interchangeable items where tracking individual units is impractical, and it approximates the physical flow of perishable goods.

points.title: Product and period costs
points.detail: Distinguishing costs added to the value of inventory from costs expensed in the period they are incurred.

questions.q: Distinguish between a product cost and a period cost, giving an example of each, and explain the test applied.
answer: A product cost is incurred to bring inventory into a condition and location ready for sale, and is added to the cost of the inventory.
Delivery in, customs duty and assembly costs are product costs, provided they can be allocated to specific units on a logical basis.
A period cost is not directly attributable to specific units and is reported as an expense in the period incurred.
Advertising, delivery out to customers and general warehouse wages are period costs.

points.title: Inventory loss, gain and write-down
points.detail: Recording differences between the inventory card and the physical stocktake, and writing inventory down to net realisable value.

questions.q: Explain the difference between an inventory loss and an inventory write-down, and the accounting treatment of each.
answer: An inventory loss occurs when the physical stocktake reveals fewer units than the inventory card shows, caused by theft, damage or recording error.
It is recorded by debiting Inventory Loss, an expense, and crediting Inventory at cost price, verified by a memo.
An inventory write-down occurs when the net realisable value of inventory falls below its cost, so the units remain but are worth less.
It is recorded by debiting Inventory Write-Down, an expense, and crediting Inventory for the difference between cost and net realisable value, which upholds faithful representation.

points.title: GST and the GST Clearing account
points.detail: GST collected on sales, GST paid on purchases, the net balance owing or receivable, and the settlement of the account.

questions.q: Explain the operation of the GST Clearing account and what a credit balance indicates.
answer: GST charged on sales is credited to GST Clearing, increasing the amount owed to the tax authority.
GST paid on purchases and expenses is debited to GST Clearing, reducing that amount.
A credit balance means GST collected exceeds GST paid, so the account is a current liability representing GST owing to the tax authority.
A debit balance means the business has paid more GST than it has collected, so the account is a current asset representing a GST refund receivable.

points.title: Drawings of inventory and advertising use
points.detail: Recording the owner taking inventory for personal use, and inventory used for advertising or donation, at cost price by memo.

questions.q: State the entry to record the owner taking inventory costing 500 dollars for personal use, and explain the reasoning.
answer: Debit Drawings 500 dollars and credit Inventory 500 dollars, verified by a memo.
The transaction is recorded at cost price because no sale has occurred and no revenue has been earned.
Drawings reduces owner's equity in accordance with the accounting entity assumption, since the benefit is personal rather than business.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Reporting and balance day adjustments
points.title: The Income Statement
points.detail: Classified presentation of revenue, cost of sales, gross profit, adjusted gross profit and other expenses to arrive at net profit.

questions.q: Explain how gross profit differs from net profit and where an inventory loss is reported.
answer: Gross profit is net sales less cost of sales, showing the margin earned on trading activity before other expenses.
Adjusted gross profit is gross profit adjusted for inventory loss or gain, since these relate directly to the trading of inventory.
Net profit is adjusted gross profit less all other expenses, including selling, administrative and financial expenses.
An inventory loss is deducted in arriving at adjusted gross profit, not treated as a general expense.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Reporting and balance day adjustments
points.title: The Balance Sheet
points.detail: Classified presentation of current and non-current assets and liabilities, and owner's equity as capital plus net profit less drawings.

questions.q: Explain the classified presentation of a Balance Sheet and how owner's equity is calculated.
answer: Assets are separated into current and non-current, as are liabilities, based on whether they will be realised or settled within 12 months.
Classification allows users to assess liquidity, by comparing current assets against current liabilities.
Owner's equity equals opening capital plus net profit less drawings for the period.
A net loss is deducted instead of profit being added, and any capital contribution during the period is also added.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Reporting and balance day adjustments
points.title: The Cash Flow Statement
points.detail: Classifying cash flows as operating, investing or financing, and reconciling to the change in the bank balance.

questions.q: Classify the following as operating, investing or financing: cash paid to creditors; purchase of a vehicle; a capital contribution by the owner; interest paid.
answer: Cash paid to creditors is an operating outflow, since it relates to the day-to-day trading activity of buying inventory.
Purchase of a vehicle is an investing outflow, since it relates to the acquisition of a non-current asset.
A capital contribution by the owner is a financing inflow, since it relates to the funding of the business.
Interest paid is an operating outflow, as it is a cost of the ordinary activities of the period.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Reporting and balance day adjustments
points.title: Cash profit and accrual profit
points.detail: Explaining why net cash flow from operations differs from net profit, and identifying the specific items causing the difference.

questions.q: Explain why a business can report a net profit but a negative net cash flow from operating activities.
answer: Profit is determined on an accrual basis, so credit sales are recognised as revenue before the cash is received from debtors.
Expenses incurred but not yet paid, such as accrued wages, reduce profit without any cash outflow in the period.
Non-cash expenses such as depreciation reduce profit but involve no payment at all.
Conversely, large payments to creditors for inventory purchased in an earlier period reduce cash without reducing profit in this period.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Reporting and balance day adjustments
points.title: Prepaid expenses
points.detail: Recording a payment in advance as an asset and transferring the consumed portion to expense at balance day.

questions.q: A business pays 12000 dollars for 12 months of insurance on 1 October. State the balance day adjustment at 31 December and the reports affected.
answer: Three months have been consumed, so the expense for the period is 3000 dollars.
Debit Insurance Expense 3000 dollars and credit Prepaid Insurance 3000 dollars, verified by a memo.
The Income Statement reports insurance expense of 3000 dollars, applying the period assumption.
The Balance Sheet reports Prepaid Insurance of 9000 dollars as a current asset, being the unconsumed future benefit.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Reporting and balance day adjustments
points.title: Accrued expenses
points.detail: Recognising an expense incurred but not yet paid at balance day, and the corresponding current liability.

questions.q: Explain why accrued wages must be recorded at balance day and state the entry.
answer: The wages relate to work already performed by employees in the current period, so the expense has been incurred.
Under the accrual basis assumption the expense is recognised when incurred, not when paid, so profit is faithfully represented.
Debit Wages Expense and credit Accrued Wages, a current liability, verified by a memo.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Reporting and balance day adjustments
points.title: Straight-line depreciation
points.detail: Calculating depreciation as cost less residual value divided by useful life, and reporting accumulated depreciation and carrying value.

questions.q: Equipment costs 50000 dollars, has a residual value of 5000 dollars and a useful life of 5 years. Calculate annual depreciation and explain the reporting treatment.
answer: Annual depreciation equals cost less residual value divided by useful life: 50000 minus 5000, divided by 5, which is 9000 dollars per year.
Debit Depreciation Expense 9000 dollars and credit Accumulated Depreciation 9000 dollars, verified by a memo.
Accumulated Depreciation is a negative asset deducted from the cost of the equipment in the Balance Sheet.
The resulting carrying value after one year is 41000 dollars, which is not intended to represent market value.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Reporting and balance day adjustments
points.title: Reducing balance depreciation
points.detail: Applying a fixed percentage to the carrying value each period, and the circumstances in which it better matches the pattern of benefit.

questions.q: Compare straight-line and reducing balance depreciation and state when reducing balance is more appropriate.
answer: Straight-line allocates an equal amount of depreciation each period, assuming benefits are consumed evenly across the asset's life.
Reducing balance applies a fixed percentage to the declining carrying value, producing a higher expense in early years and lower in later years.
Reducing balance is more appropriate where the asset contributes more in its early years or where repair costs rise as it ages.
The choice affects the pattern of reported profit but not the total depreciation charged over the asset's life.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Extension of recording and reporting
points.title: Acquiring a non-current asset
points.detail: Determining the cost of a non-current asset by including all costs necessary to bring it to a location and condition ready for use.

questions.q: A machine is purchased for 30000 dollars with delivery of 1200 dollars, installation of 2000 dollars and first-year insurance of 900 dollars. Calculate the cost of the asset.
answer: The cost includes all costs incurred to bring the asset to a location and condition ready for use.
Delivery of 1200 dollars and installation of 2000 dollars are therefore included in the cost of the asset.
Insurance of 900 dollars is an ongoing operating cost of using the asset, not a cost of acquiring it, so it is a period expense.
The cost of the machine is 30000 plus 1200 plus 2000, which is 33200 dollars.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Extension of recording and reporting
points.title: Disposal of a non-current asset
points.detail: Removing the asset and its accumulated depreciation, recognising proceeds and calculating the profit or loss on disposal.

questions.q: Explain how a profit or loss on disposal of a non-current asset arises and what it indicates.
answer: The carrying value at the date of disposal is the cost less accumulated depreciation to that date, including depreciation for the part-year.
Profit or loss on disposal is the proceeds received less that carrying value.
A loss indicates the asset was depreciated too slowly, meaning the useful life or residual value estimate was too generous.
A profit indicates it was depreciated too quickly; both arise because depreciation is an estimate, not a valuation.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Extension of recording and reporting
points.title: Accrued revenue
points.detail: Recognising revenue earned but not yet received at balance day, and the corresponding current asset.

questions.q: Explain the treatment of accrued revenue at balance day and state the entry.
answer: Revenue that has been earned in the period but not yet received must be recognised under the accrual basis assumption.
Debit Accrued Revenue, a current asset, and credit the relevant revenue account, verified by a memo.
The Income Statement reports the full amount earned and the Balance Sheet reports the amount still to be received.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Extension of recording and reporting
points.title: Prepaid revenue
points.detail: Recording cash received in advance as a liability and recognising revenue only as the obligation is satisfied.

questions.q: Explain why cash received in advance from a customer is recorded as a liability rather than revenue.
answer: The business has received the cash but has not yet provided the goods or services, so the revenue has not been earned.
An obligation exists to provide those goods or services, or to refund the customer, which meets the definition of a liability.
Revenue is recognised progressively as the obligation is satisfied, transferring the amount from Prepaid Revenue to the revenue account.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Extension of recording and reporting
points.title: Closing the ledger and the Profit and Loss Summary
points.detail: Closing revenue and expense accounts to the Profit and Loss Summary, transferring net profit to Capital, and closing Drawings.

questions.q: Explain the purpose of closing entries and identify which accounts are closed.
answer: Closing entries reset revenue and expense accounts to zero so the next period's figures are recorded separately, applying the period assumption.
Revenue accounts are debited and the Profit and Loss Summary credited; expense accounts are credited and the Summary debited.
The balance of the Profit and Loss Summary, being net profit or loss, is transferred to the Capital account.
Drawings is also closed to Capital, while asset, liability and equity accounts are balanced and carried forward rather than closed.

points.title: The purpose of budgeting
points.detail: Planning future activity, setting targets, allocating resources, anticipating cash shortfalls and providing a benchmark against which to assess performance.

questions.q: Explain three benefits a small business gains from preparing budgeted reports.
answer: Budgets identify likely cash shortfalls in advance, so finance can be arranged before the shortage occurs.
They set measurable targets against which actual results can later be compared, enabling variance analysis.
They assist decision making by modelling the financial effect of a proposed change before it is committed to.
They also coordinate activity, since purchasing, staffing and marketing plans must be consistent with the budgeted level of sales.

points.title: Budgeted Cash Flow Statement
points.detail: Forecasting receipts from debtors and payments to creditors using expected collection and payment patterns, and projecting the closing bank balance.

questions.q: Explain how receipts from debtors are estimated in a Budgeted Cash Flow Statement.
answer: Begin with the opening balance of Debtors Control, which is expected to be collected in the budget period.
Add budgeted credit sales for the period, including GST, since that is the amount customers will pay.
Apply the expected collection pattern, so only the proportion expected to be received in the period is included.
Deduct any expected discount expense or bad debts, and the remainder of credit sales becomes the closing debtors balance.

points.title: Budgeted Income Statement
points.detail: Forecasting sales, cost of sales and expenses on an accrual basis, and distinguishing budgeted profit from budgeted cash flow.

questions.q: Explain why the sales figure in a Budgeted Income Statement differs from receipts from debtors in a Budgeted Cash Flow Statement.
answer: Budgeted sales are recognised when the sale is expected to occur, on an accrual basis, and exclude GST.
Receipts from debtors are recognised when cash is expected to be received, include GST, and include collections of prior period sales.
The two therefore differ in timing, in the treatment of GST and in the inclusion of cash sales and opening debtors.

points.title: Budgeted Balance Sheet
points.detail: Projecting closing balances of assets, liabilities and owner's equity from the budgeted income and cash flow statements.

questions.q: Explain how the closing Capital figure in a Budgeted Balance Sheet is derived.
answer: Begin with the opening Capital balance from the actual Balance Sheet at the start of the period.
Add budgeted net profit from the Budgeted Income Statement, and add any expected capital contribution.
Deduct budgeted drawings for the period to arrive at the closing Capital figure.

points.title: Variance reports
points.detail: Comparing actual with budgeted results, classifying variances as favourable or unfavourable, and investigating the causes.

questions.q: Explain how a variance is classified as favourable or unfavourable, and why an unfavourable expense variance is not always a problem.
answer: A variance is favourable when the actual result improves profit relative to budget, such as higher revenue or lower expenses.
It is unfavourable when the actual result reduces profit relative to budget.
An unfavourable expense variance may be acceptable if it accompanies a favourable sales variance, since higher sales require higher variable costs.
Variances should therefore be investigated in relation to one another and to the level of activity actually achieved, not in isolation.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Analysis and decision making
points.title: Profitability indicators
points.detail: Gross profit margin, net profit margin, return on owner's investment and return on assets, and the interpretation of each.

questions.q: Explain what gross profit margin and net profit margin measure, and what a falling net profit margin with a stable gross profit margin indicates.
answer: Gross profit margin is gross profit divided by net sales, expressed as a percentage, measuring the margin earned on trading.
Net profit margin is net profit divided by net sales, measuring the proportion of each sales dollar retained after all expenses.
A stable gross profit margin indicates the mark-up and cost of inventory are unchanged.
A falling net profit margin therefore indicates other expenses have risen relative to sales, so the investigation should focus on operating expenses rather than pricing or supplier costs.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Analysis and decision making
points.title: Liquidity indicators
points.detail: Working capital ratio and quick asset ratio, their calculation and the distinction between them.

questions.q: Distinguish between the working capital ratio and the quick asset ratio and explain why both are useful.
answer: The working capital ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities, measuring the ability to meet short-term debts as they fall due.
The quick asset ratio excludes inventory and prepaid expenses from current assets, and excludes bank overdraft from current liabilities.
Inventory is excluded because it must first be sold and the resulting debt collected before it becomes cash.
A business with an adequate working capital ratio but a poor quick asset ratio is holding a large amount of slow-moving inventory and may struggle to pay debts promptly.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Analysis and decision making
points.title: Efficiency indicators
points.detail: Inventory turnover, debtors turnover, creditors turnover and asset turnover, and what each reveals about management of resources.

questions.q: Explain what inventory turnover measures and the risks of a turnover that is too slow or too fast.
answer: Inventory turnover measures the average number of days taken to sell inventory, calculated using average inventory divided by cost of sales multiplied by 365.
A slow turnover ties up cash in stock, increases storage and insurance costs and raises the risk of obsolescence or write-down.
A very fast turnover may indicate insufficient inventory is being held, risking stockouts and lost sales.
The appropriate figure depends on the nature of the goods, since perishables must turn over far faster than durable items.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Analysis and decision making
points.title: Relationships between indicators
points.detail: Analysing how turnover, margin and liquidity interact, and avoiding conclusions based on a single indicator.

questions.q: A business reduces its selling price, and gross profit margin falls while inventory turnover improves and net profit rises. Explain this outcome.
answer: Reducing the selling price lowers the margin earned on each unit, so gross profit margin falls.
The lower price increases sales volume, so inventory is sold more quickly and turnover improves.
Because more units are sold, total gross profit can rise even though the margin per unit is lower.
Fixed expenses are spread across more sales, so net profit rises; the indicators must be read together rather than judged individually.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Analysis and decision making
points.title: Strategies to improve performance
points.detail: Recommending specific strategies to improve profitability, liquidity or efficiency, and evaluating the trade-offs of each.

questions.q: Recommend two strategies to improve a slow debtors turnover and evaluate one of them.
answer: Offer a settlement discount for early payment, which gives customers a financial incentive to pay sooner.
Tighten credit terms and enforce them with reminders, statements and stop-supply for overdue accounts.
A settlement discount improves cash flow and reduces the risk of bad debts, but the discount expense reduces net profit.
Tightening terms preserves margin but risks losing customers to competitors offering more generous credit, so the effect on sales must be weighed.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Analysis and decision making
points.title: Non-financial information and ethical considerations
points.detail: Using non-financial data in decisions, and considering the social and environmental consequences of accounting decisions.

questions.q: Explain why non-financial information matters in decision making and give two examples, plus one ethical consideration.
answer: Financial reports record only what can be measured in monetary terms, so they omit factors that affect future performance.
Examples include customer satisfaction levels, staff turnover, the number of repeat customers and environmental compliance.
These predict future revenue and cost, so a decision based solely on this period's profit may damage long-term performance.

An ethical consideration is whether a strategy such as sourcing cheaper inventory relies on poor labour or environmental practices, which carries reputational and moral consequences beyond the reported figures.

points.title: Showing workings and using correct formats
points.detail: Presenting calculations clearly, using correct report headings and classifications, and including narrations and dates where required.

questions.q: Explain why workings should be shown even when a single figure is requested.
answer: Method marks are available for the correct approach even when the final figure is incorrect.
Without workings, an incorrect answer earns nothing and the examiner cannot identify where the error occurred.
Clear workings also let you check your own calculation quickly if the figure appears implausible.

points.title: Explaining and justifying answers
points.detail: Answering theory questions with reference to the specific assumption, qualitative characteristic or definition, and applying it to the scenario given.

questions.q: Explain the structure of a strong response to a question asking you to justify a treatment with reference to an accounting assumption.
answer: Name the relevant assumption or qualitative characteristic precisely.
State its definition briefly and accurately.
Apply it to the specific transaction in the question, referring to the actual figures and items given.
State the consequence for the reports, such as which report is affected and in what direction.

points.title: Common errors
points.detail: Reversing debits and credits, recording at selling price instead of cost, omitting GST, misclassifying current and non-current items and forgetting the second entry for a sale.

questions.q: Name four common errors in Accounting responses and state how to avoid each.
answer: Recording inventory at selling price rather than cost when it is withdrawn or lost; check whether a sale has actually occurred.
Omitting the cost of sales entry for a credit sale; remember every sale of inventory requires two entries.
Including GST in the Income Statement; GST affects the GST Clearing account and never revenue or expenses.
Misclassifying items as current or non-current; apply the 12-month test to each item, including splitting loan repayments.
